loc: Lesson04_Maintaining_Veeam_Kasten_Over_Time.html · Section "Watching Veeam Kasten itself", Layer two: the built-in Prometheus instance — first PromQL code block
prop: Read it as: how many backup actions finished successfully in the last 24 hours. action_ended_total is the metric name; the curly braces filter to backup actions that succeeded; [24h] is the lookback window; increase counts how many happened inside it; sum and round collapse that down to one tidy number.
why: Every shell/Helm command elsewhere in this course gets a plain-English translation immediately after it — the Helm install caption literally says "read it as three sentences." The first PromQL query in this section (sum(round(increase(action_ended_total{action="backup",state="succeeded"}[24h])))) breaks that pattern: it gets no caption at all, and the second query only gets a one-line statement of its *purpose*, not its syntax. For a GUI-preferring learner with zero Prometheus background, this is a wall of unexplained syntax in a course that otherwise never leaves one — a confidence-curve break specific to this section. I could still follow the module's actual operational point (create the two recommended alerts) without decoding the query, but I couldn't have written a third alert myself. Note: PromQL syntax is generic Prometheus behavior, not a Kasten-specific claim, so this addition needs no product citation.

prop: so if the platform team moves the cluster first, your options narrow to whichever Veeam Kasten release supports the new version, while upgrading Veeam Kasten first keeps the choice. This is the coordination cost a Veeam Data Platform administrator does not carry when the backup server owns its own Windows host. Put a name on it: agree with the platform team, in writing, who has to sign off before a cluster upgrade proceeds if it would drop the running Veeam Kasten release out of the supported matrix — otherwise the backup platform loses support status by nobody's decision.
why: The module correctly identifies a real coordination cost between the backup team and the platform team that owns the cluster, but stops at naming the risk without naming who is accountable for resolving it. A director finishing this section could not say who owns the escalation when the two calendars conflict, which is exactly the ownership-blur this persona is scoped to catch.

loc: Lesson04_Maintaining_Veeam_Kasten_Over_Time.html · Monitoring section, "Layer three: your existing monitoring stack"
orig: Grafana then visualizes what Prometheus collected, and alerts fire when metrics cross the levels you care about [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093].
prop: Grafana then visualizes what Prometheus collected, and alerts fire when metrics cross the levels you care about [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1093]. In most organizations that central Prometheus/Grafana stack belongs to a platform or observability team rather than the backup team — name who owns wiring the two alerts this module recommends (failed actions, catalog space over 50%) before you assume they already exist.
why: The module gives excellent proof-of-health guidance (the two alerts to create first) but frames wiring them up as something 'you' do, without acknowledging that in a typical enterprise the monitoring stack these alerts ride on is owned by a separate team. A director reading this section could not say whose backlog those two alerts land on.

orig: The KDR passphrase is retrievable by someone other than you, from a passphrase provider rather than a personal note [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.572].
prop: The KDR passphrase is retrievable by someone other than you, from a passphrase provider rather than a personal note [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.572]. Decide who that second person or team is — security, a fellow backup admin, the secrets-management team — and write it into the runbook; 'someone other than you' is a decision your team has to make explicitly, not a default the product supplies.
why: This is the single most important resilience control in the course (the catalog cannot be recovered without it) and the module correctly flags that a second party must be able to retrieve it, but never names who that should be. Left as-is, a team could satisfy the letter of the guidance ('someone other than you') without ever having a real answer to who that is, which defeats the point.

loc: Lesson04_Maintaining_Veeam_Kasten_Over_Time.html · Section 02 ("Keeping pace with Kubernetes") and Section 03 ("Check the platform's own plumbing with k10tools")
orig: The k10tools binary has commands that help validate whether a cluster is set up correctly before installing Veeam Kasten and debug the Veeam Kasten micro services [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.864].
prop: Add the command to obtain/install the k10tools binary the first time it is referenced (either here or back in Module 03, before `./k10tools primer upgrade` is first shown), in the same copy-pasteable style used for the primer and debug curl commands.
why: `k10tools` is invoked directly in at least three places across Modules 03–04 (`./k10tools primer upgrade`, `k10tools frs`, the storage-class validation reference) but the module never shows how the binary gets onto the machine running these commands. I would stall at the very first `./k10tools` invocation with no idea where the executable came from.
